title: EIA Weekly Petroleum Status Report highlights, week ending 2026-10-09
text:
[Compiled on 2026-10-25 from EIA's archived WPSR tables for the week ending October 9, 2026 (released Thursday 2026-10-15, delayed by the Columbus Day holiday): https://www.eia.gov/petroleum/supply/weekly/archive/2026/2026_10_15/csv/table1.csv and table2.csv, saved alongside this file. EIA's archived highlights.pdf for this week carries the narrative text of the week ending September 11 (an EIA archive error), so no EIA narrative is quoted here; its tables match the figures below.]

For the week ending October 9, 2026, U.S. refineries processed 16,615 thousand b/d of crude oil, up 135 thousand b/d from the previous week, at 93.5% capacity utilization (92.7% the previous week).

Crude oil imports decreased 791 thousand b/d to 6,049 thousand b/d. Crude oil exports decreased 195 thousand b/d to 4,570 thousand b/d. Domestic crude oil production decreased 300 thousand b/d to 13,679 thousand b/d.

Commercial crude oil inventories (excluding the Strategic Petroleum Reserve) decreased 8.557 million barrels to 415.577 million barrels. Total motor gasoline inventories increased 3.518 million barrels to 208.262 million barrels. Distillate fuel oil inventories decreased 2.527 million barrels to 102.611 million barrels. Kerosene-type jet fuel inventories increased 0.291 million barrels to 42.795 million barrels. Propane/propylene inventories decreased 1.471 million barrels. The SPR was unchanged at 282.983 million barrels. Total stocks excluding the SPR decreased 13.384 million barrels.

Year-ago comparison (week ending October 10, 2025): commercial crude 423.785 million barrels; gasoline 218.826; distillate 117.030; SPR 407.745.

Not available from the archived tables: Cushing stocks (EIA API series W_EPC0_SAX_YCUOK_MBBL: 26.607 million barrels, +1.862), product supplied, and EIA's "% vs five-year average" statements.

title: Our 2010–2024 study of inventories and WTI curve structure
text:
Weekly sample 2010-01-08 – 2024-03-29 (743 WPSR weeks). Prices taken at the Wednesday WPSR release date (prior trading day if a holiday). Inventory variables are **actual** weekly changes; without consensus forecasts these are not surprises, and the results are associations, not causal estimates.
1. **Stock levels explain curve structure; weekly changes barely do.** Deviations of Cushing and total US crude stocks from seasonal norms explain 36% of the variation in WTI M1–M2, with Cushing the stronger variable: each 1 mb of Cushing below normal goes with ~$0.029/bbl more backwardation, and the tightest Cushing quartile was backwardated 82% of the time vs 1% in the loosest.
2. **Weekly inventory changes have the expected sign but little explanatory power** (R² 0.03 for the spread, 0.03 for returns). A 1 mb Cushing draw goes with ~$0.031/bbl spread tightening; headline crude changes are not significant for the spread. Without consensus data, these are actual changes, not surprises.
3. **No significant evidence that Cushing changes matter more when Cushing is tight** (interaction p = 0.19). The point estimate has the expected sign, but the data do not support claiming a regime difference.
4. **Brent–WTI is wider when Cushing is tight and US exports are high** (2016+), consistent with WTI pricing as the export barrel that has to move overseas; this is an association.
